notes: On 15 January 2025, impeached President Yoon Suk-yeol was apprehended by the Corruption Investigation Office for High-ranking Officials (CIO) for questioning over insurrection charges related to his martial law declaration on 3 December (coded at Seoul City). Yoon has faced trial on charges including insurrection, abuse of authority, obstruction of official duties, falsifying official documents, perjury, and alleged violations of the Political Funds Act and the Public Official Election Act. The charges also include allegations that he failed to properly convene a full cabinet meeting before declaring martial law, attempted to heighten inter-Korean tensions to justify the decree, and interfered with investigations, including alleged undue influence in the Marine Corps investigation into the death of a conscripted soldier. Among these cases, the first ruling was delivered on 16 January 2026, when a court sentenced him to five years in prison in connection with findings related to obstructing the execution of an arrest warrant, irregularities in cabinet deliberation procedures prior to the martial law declaration, and issues surrounding the creation and handling of an official martial law document. In a separate trial concerning the insurrection charges related to the martial law declaration, prosecutors sought the death penalty, arguing that he had led actions that undermined constitutional order. On 19 February 2026, the Seoul Central District Court sentenced him to life imprisonment, finding that the declaration of martial law and related actions constituted insurrection. On 9 July 2026, the Supreme Court upheld a seven-year prison sentence against Yoon on charges including special obstruction of official duties, abuse of authority, violations of the Presidential Records Act, damaging official documents, and falsifying official documents, making it the first final ruling among the cases arising from the 3 December martial law declaration. On 13 July 2026, the Seoul Central District Court sentenced Yoon to two years in prison in a first-instance ruling for violating the Political Funds Act by accepting free public opinion polling services in exchange for helping secure a party nomination for a candidate in the 2022 by-elections.
